fields.sample_size: 22 months of fieldwork in Sao Paulo between 2013 and 2016, with a reference point in the eastern periphery; about 45 semi-structured interviews with water professionals, state officials (DAEE, the housing and urban development company, state and municipal environment secretariats) and neighbourhood activists; informal conversations, walking tours, observation of meetings and discursive analysis of texts and policy documents
fields.effect_measure: qualitative political-ecology case study (interviews, observation, document analysis); descriptive figures from utility and press sources; no quantitative estimate
fields.effect_estimate: Rainfall in the Cantareira catchment was 444 mm in the 2013-14 rainy season against an average 995 mm, and by January 2015 the reservoir stood at 7% capacity. Instead of formal rationing (a plan discussed in January 2015 of four days without water for two with water), SABESP used pressure reductions in the pipes (in use since the 1990s; about 30% of water is lost through leaks) and a bill discount (30% for cutting use by 20%, February-November 2014); the utility's president said fewer than 1% of residents lost water for days, but shortages were felt throughout the city and fell disproportionately on the urban periphery where homes lack storage tanks (caixas); a rise in waterborne diarrhoea in 2014-15 was linked to use of the reservoir dead volume. The author argues that unequal outcomes came from infrastructural histories and the choice of pressure management over declared rationing, which obscured who went without water.
fields.section: Accepted author manuscript (Manchester repository, about 30 pages): Introduction; Methods (22 months fieldwork); the 2014-2015 crisis and response; pressure reductions and the periphery; Conclusion
fields.exact_location: Methods (fieldwork and 45 interviews, p. 12); section 3 (crisis and response, pressure reductions); Conclusion; Political Geography 65

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a qualitative political-ecology case study of the Sao Paulo state government's response to the 2014-2015 water crisis (22 months fieldwork, about 45 interviews, document analysis); read in full text 2026-10-04. Descriptive figures quoted from utility and press sources.
